metadata.title: What Comes First When You Hire Abroad?
metadata.purpose: Answer what a legal/HR team must decide before drafting an employment contract for a first hire in a new country: how the role is classified and who the legal employer will be, not the contract itself. Lands the carry-out that the contract can't fix a bad classification -- the country's labor law decides who counts as an employee, not the page.

beats.narration_text: Someone on a legal team wants to hire their first person in Germany. Wrong first move: draft a contract. What they actually need first is the worker's classification. Liam, take them through it.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'What contract do we need to hire someone in Germany?', hesitates on 'contract', corrects to 'classification', lands the real question

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('contract' -> 'classification') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: You could draft an employment contract today, calling the role whatever you like. But a contract's label doesn't decide the classification -- the country's labor law does. Call someone a contractor while you set their hours, hand them your equipment, and take them as their only client, and a local court will call them an employee anyway, no matter what the page says.

shot.new_visual_element: A contract card with an editable 'CONTRACTOR' label; behind it, clock/toolbox/single-client icons all light up employee-shaped anyway; a stamp comes down over the label reading EMPLOYEE

production_viz.label: The label doesn't decide the classification
production_viz.mechanic: A card headed 'CONTRACT' with a text field reading 'CONTRACTOR' in its header. Three status icons beneath it -- a clock, a toolbox, a single-client badge -- fade in and light up one at a time, all employee-shaped, while the header label stays unchanged. A stamp shape comes down over the header anyway, marking 'EMPLOYEE' in accent color. A caption fades in beneath: 'the page doesn't decide this.'

beats.narration_text: A real hiring plan runs three checks before any contract gets written: how the role is classified, who will be the legal employer on paper -- your own entity, or an Employer of Record standing in for one -- and which local rules are mandatory no matter what the contract says, like notice periods and statutory benefits. Watch the anchor: a developer in Berlin, forty hours a week, one client, using your laptop and your tools.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- three check chips lighting in turn (classification / legal employer / mandatory terms), then a dim, icon-only developer card set off to the side

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- three checks, then the unclassified hire
production_viz.mechanic: Three chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a check (CLASSIFICATION / LEGAL EMPLOYER / MANDATORY TERMS), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. A single card appears off to the side, dim and outlined only, reading 'developer -- Berlin' with icon-only marks (clock, laptop, single-client badge) and no fields filled in -- visibly incomplete against the three-check shape just shown. THIS EXACT CARD RETURNS, FILLED IN, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Run the Berlin developer through the checks: full control over their hours, one client, your equipment -- that's employee-shaped, no matter what the contract calls them. Passing as contractor-shaped today doesn't mean it stays that way; change how the work actually runs and the classification can flip later, same contract. And landing on employee doesn't mean you need your own German entity tomorrow -- an Employer of Record can be the legal employer on paper while you sort that out.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the dim developer card lighting up with all three checks filled and moving into the main list; then split into 'classification can still flip' and 'doesn't require your own entity'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- classified, not locked in
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 DIM CARD RETURNS, identical placement, and fills in one field at a time (classification: employee-shaped / legal employer: entity or EOR / mandatory terms: notice + benefits) until fully lit, then slides into a row alongside other completed entries. It splits into two cards: left reads 'contractor-shaped today' with a struck-through 'LOCKED IN' beneath it labelled 'classification can still flip'; right reads 'employee-shaped' with a faint 'Employer of Record available' card at its edge labelled 'doesn't require your own entity'.

beats.narration_text: The contract can't fix a bad classification. Work out how the role is classified and who the legal employer will be before you draft anything -- the country's labor law decides that, not the label on the page.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt -- read it with me. I'm planning to hire our first employee in a new country. Before drafting anything, walk me through how the role would likely be classified there under local labor law, the difference between opening our own entity there versus using an Employer of Record, and which statutory terms -- notice period, benefits, termination rules -- would apply once it's classified. Liam, in for Bear.
